An early name for the followers of Jesus and their way of life (9:2, 19:9, 24:14).
Greek astheneia, frailty, sickness, lack of strength. The world's reason to despise Paul, and the place of Christ's power: “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (12:10).
Jonah's flight is a descent: down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the sea (1:3, 5).
The Persian province of which Judah was a small part, the lands beyond the river as seen from Persia (4:10; 5:3).
The faith handed to Timothy to guard, like money left with a trusted friend (6:20).
Greek parathēkē, a deposit left in trust. The gospel given to Timothy to guard (1:14).
The meaning of Micah's name, echoed in the closing hymn (7:18).
In Hebrew almanah, the model of the person left without protection or provision. The city has ‘become a widow’ (1:1).
The Hebrew kanaph means a wing or the corner of a garment. Ruth shelters under God's wings (2:12) and asks for the corner of Boaz's garment (3:9).
In Hebrew chokmah, skill for living, from craftsmanship to governing to moral judgment. God gave it to Solomon as a gift (4:29).
Greek sophia. Corinth's wisdom meant clever speech, learning and status. God's wisdom is the crucified Christ, who “has become for us wisdom from God” (1:30).
In Hebrew maskilim, those with insight who instruct many and lead many to righteousness (11:33; 12:3).
In Hebrew chamal means to spare or have pity. The poem says three times that God acted without it (2:2, 17, 21), and that is the heart of the city's anguish.
Greek martus. One who tells what he has seen. The apostles are witnesses of the risen Jesus (1:8, 1:22); the word later came to mean martyr.
Greek martus, one who testifies; later, a martyr (1:5; 2:13).
In Hebrew hoy, the cry of a funeral lament, spoken over the living as if they were already dead (5:8-22).
Hoy, the funeral cry, raised over the city of blood (3:1).
Greek logos. God's speech, by which the world was made; in John, a name for the Son, who was with God and was God (1:1, 1:14).
The Hebrew melakhah, used for the rebuilding throughout. The enemies want to stop the work, and the people keep returning to it (4:6; 6:3).
Deeds done in obedience to the law of Moses (3:20, 3:28). Read as any effort to earn standing with God, or above all as the marks of being Jewish, such as circumcision.
Deeds the law of Moses requires. Read as any effort to earn God's favour, or above all as the marks of Jewish identity such as circumcision. See the part above.
Greek erga, things done. For James, deeds of faith and mercy, like feeding the hungry (2:14-26).
Often in John, people organized against God. Yet it is the world God loves (3:16, 15:18).
Greek sarkikos, living by merely human ways. Paul says jealousy and quarrels show it: “Are you not walking in the way of man?” (3:3).
God's settled opposition to evil, which will come on the Day of the Lord. Jesus is ‘our deliverer from the coming wrath’ (1:10).
To argue a case or decide it. Its participle in 9:33 names an umpire, a mediator who could lay his hand on both sides.
Sea of reeds, the Hebrew name English Bibles give as the Red Sea (13:18). Where Israel crossed is not known.
To fear or revere. The fear of God runs through the book (5:7) and is its conclusion (12:13).
Every seventh year, when debts were cancelled and the law was read aloud to all Israel (15:1-2; 31:10-11).
Fear. The fear of the LORD is reverence, awe and trust that shows itself in obedience, the beginning of knowledge (1:7; 9:10).
Gain, advantage or profit, a word found in the Old Testament only in Ecclesiastes. What does a man gain? (1:3)
The beam that bound an animal to its work, and a picture of a king's demands. Rehoboam promised a heavier one (12:14).
The ram's horn, and so the Jubilee, the fiftieth year announced by its blast (25:9-10).
To act as a prostitute: the book's main picture of Israel's unfaithfulness, from the wife of harlotries (1:2) onward.
Seed or offspring. Like ‘seed’ in English it can mean one child or a whole line. It runs from 3:15 through every promise to Abraham's family.
First the Jebusite fortress David captured (5:7), then the City of David, the temple hill, Jerusalem, and God's people.
The hill of Jerusalem where the temple stood, and so a name for Jerusalem and for God's dwelling among his people. It appears 38 times in the Psalms.
The hill of the temple, and Jerusalem itself, the city God judges and will restore (2:3; 40:9; 62:1).
The hill of Jerusalem where the temple stood, and the city itself, where the LORD dwells (2:1; 3:17, 21).
Jerusalem's hill and the city itself. It will be plowed (3:12), and the nations will come to it (4:2).
